messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 18
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 59

She is eighteen years old, a first-year architecture student at the university, and she still takes the bus even though the stop is three blocks from the building where it happened.

She was walking to her studio that afternoon in early autumn, carrying a tube of blueprints she had stayed up all night to finish. The street was busy, the usual noise of the city. A man was crossing the intersection ahead of her, slightly ahead of the pedestrian signal. She noticed him because he was carrying a small child on his shoulders, a girl with a bright pink backpack. The child was laughing, reaching up toward the leaves of the trees that lined the sidewalk. She remembers the exact shade of pink of that backpack because she had a similar one when she was small.

The truck came from the left, running a red light. She heard the engine first, a sudden roar, then the impact. It was not a loud sound, she sometimes tells herself. It was a wet, dense thud, like a heavy book falling onto a concrete floor. The child was thrown forward, away from the man. The man was not thrown. He was pulled under.

She remembers screaming. She remembers the child’s pink backpack lying in the gutter, still moving a little as the girl tried to sit up. She remembers the driver getting out of the truck, a man in a blue uniform, his hands on his head, walking in circles. She remembers someone saying, “Don’t look, don’t look,” and she did not look at the space under the truck. But she knows what she did not see, and that is worse. She sees it anyway, every night, in the fifteen minutes between closing her eyes and the moment she forces them open again.

That was eight months ago.

Now she cannot take the bus past that intersection. She walks an extra twenty minutes in the cold, even when it rains, even when her boots are soaked. She has mapped three different routes to the architecture building, none of which cross a major street with traffic lights. She tells her professors she prefers the exercise.

In studio class, she struggles to draw. Her line work has become jagged, hesitant. When she tries to sketch a pedestrian plaza, she finds herself erasing the figures, leaving the benches empty. Her professor asks why her elevations have no people, and she says she wants the buildings to speak for themselves. She knows this is not true. When she looks at a human figure on a page, even a stick figure with a circle for a head, she sees the girl with the pink backpack, and her hand stops moving.

She started carrying a small notebook in her bag, separate from her sketchbooks. In it she writes the date and time of every intrusive image, every sudden feeling of falling, every moment she hears the wet sound again. She has filled three notebooks. She keeps them in a shoebox under her bed and never opens them after she writes. She does not know why she does this. She does not know why she cannot throw them away.

She has stopped going to the architecture library after dark because the fluorescent lights buzz the same way the truck’s engine did in the seconds before. The buzz is not the same, she knows that rationally. But when she hears it, her chest tightens, her hands get cold, and she needs to leave. She has left three exams early this semester. She tells her classmates she is sick. They believe her because she looks tired.

She has not told anyone what she saw. Not her mother, who calls every Friday and asks if she is eating well. Not her roommate, who once asked why she never wants to walk to the coffee shop on the corner. She does not know how to start. She thinks if she says it out loud, the sound will come back, and this time she will not be able to stop screaming.

At night, she lies on her back in the dark and traces the outline of windows onto the ceiling with her finger, imagining the plans of a building with no doors, no stairs, no intersection outside. A place where no one can enter and no one can leave. She is still trying to design it. She has filled an entire roll of tracing paper with sketches of that building, and she cannot finish any of them.
